My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

📅 2025-07-01  |  Read Source →

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

Gilbert Ott is an ever curious traveler and one of the world's leading travel experts. His adventures take him all over the globe, often spanning over 200,000 miles a year and his travel exploits are regularly... More by Gilbert Ott

Good thing you did the Edit deal as the Thompson doesn’t honor Hyatt Globalist benefits. So, no upgrade and no breakfast for Globalists.

Not true (unless something changed) stayed here in May 2023 and got Globalist benefits

Am I the only one finding Edit hotels are north of $1000 a night? Whatever the credit Chase is giving is for staying at an Edit property isn’t enough to offset the exceptionally high rate.

I’ve stayed at that Thompson many times and been upgraded to suites and the Upper Stories. The previous poster is empirically wrong.

doesn’t Edit usually require a two night minimum? How did you get the benefits for only a one night stay?

I had thought I read that the benefits are for stays of at least 2 nights. Is that incorrect?

Actually – just looked up what I read and I think it’s the $250 credit every six months that requires a 2-night stay but not the other benefits. So looks like you could have spent 12,500 points + $250 cash for a second night and gotten the $250 credited back.

How to Navigate the Tariff Circus

📅 2025-06-13  |  Read Source →

Quite accidentally, it looks like we timed our last talk about the stock market pretty darned well. Back in February 2025, the market put the perfect cap on a multi year climb before stepping onto the wild roller coaster we’re currently riding. Since then it has seen some of the steepest drops and recoveries in history, losing a full 20% of its value at the bottom while somehow managing to end up right back near the peak as I’m writing this.

And although stock market volatility doesn’t always come with an easily labeled explanation, this time the reason seems pretty clear: it’s the Tariffs.

As our financial world has been whipped around like a circus tent in a hurricane for the last several months, almost everyone who has a stake in this country has been wondering what to make of it.

As I write this, we still don’t know the outcome of the worldwide tariff and trade battle that our unpredictable government has unleashed upon the world. But we’re already seeing the results: businesses are bracing for massive changes, currencies and interest rates are reacting, and regular investors like you and me are wondering what the future holds for our early retirement funds. Surveying my own group of friends, the reactions span the whole range of emotions from “this is a giant Nothingburger” to “we’re all totally screwed.”

So what’s the real answer? To get closer to that, we should start with the most basic question of:

A tariff is just a sales tax charged by our government on goods which are imported into the country.  They are paid by whoever is doing the importing – meaning you if you order something like an e-bike directly from a company in China, or by companies like Amazon, Walmart, or Apple which import products from other countries by the shipload.

But in the end, the tariffs aren’t paid by China or Amazon or Apple. They are paid by you, the end consumer, because if their cost of goods increases, a retailer is of course going to raise their prices to continue to make a profit.

Tariffs also affect companies directly: if Home Depot wants to build a new store or Chevron needs a new oil rig, the tariffs on imported steel, copper, lumber and a million other components will raise the cost of these construction projects. And they raise the cost of housing, because most of the building materials in houses come from multiple countries as well.

On average, tariffs will result in higher prices for everything just like any other broad-based sales tax. And just like most other taxes, the overall effect is to slow the economy and reduce our spending power. On the positive side, all that tax money flows into the government’s pocket which could help fund the national budget and even reduce the deficit.

Of course, every government needs at least some tax revenue to function, so it makes sense to use some mix of sales, income and corporate taxes to get there. The most important part is that the levels need to be as low as possible while still keeping the country running well, and as fair and predictable as possible, so that people and businesses have an incentive to work hard and the ability to plan far into the future.

And that’s where our current tariff regime gets it completely backwards. Donald Trump is throwing around random, extremely high tariff numbers as threats, then walking them back and changing them on an almost daily basis..

Whoa, that Sounds Mostly Bad – Is There a Good Side of Tariffs?

Sometimes, a country will use tariffs to protect their own domestic industries. For example, if you put a tax on imported Hondas, then General Motors cars will gain a competitive advantage – so GM will make more money. In this example, most consumers end up losing due to increased prices and decreased selection. But at least domestic auto manufacturers and their employees are happy.

This can be strategic (for example we might want to slap a tax on imported fighter jets to make sure Boeing and Lockheed can remain in business, for national defense purposes.) Or it can be corrupt (a politician might receive funding from kingpins in the steel industry, and in return then push through tariffs on imported steel to protect the profits of US steelmakers.)

And this isn’t just a Trump or Republican thing either – Joe Biden used tariffs during his terms in an attempt to please swing-state voters. One of the worst examples was a tax on imported solar panel components (which Trump has since raised even further, proving that Boneheadedness can be Bipartisan). These are sheets of cheap glass that literally pump the cheapest energy and easiest wealth into your country for 30 years as soon as you plug them in. Cheap energy lowers everyone’s cost of living while also boosting industry. There is no good reason to block such wealth from flowing across your borders.

Let’s go back to that hypothetical tax on Hondas, and let’s say it’s a big one like $5000. At that level, many buyers will start heading over to the GM dealer next door to consider what he’s selling. Sure, the GM cars may not be as good, but for five grand some people are going to settle in order to save some money.

Because of this, GM’s sales go up. So they hire more employees and build more factories. They might even develop some new models and new technologies in response to all that new demand. More people learn advanced skills and in the best case it becomes a virtuous circle.

But in exchange for this boom in the auto industry, everyone else has to pay more for slightly shittier cars and trucks. Higher vehicle prices means Amazon will have to spend more on their delivery fleet, so they will raise prices slightly on everything they sell. Somewhere a startup company or a medical breakthrough will be just a bit less likely to happen, because they are operating in an environment that is just a bit more expensive and a bit less efficient.

On top of that, with GM liberated from the hassle of competing with Honda, it will have less incentive to innovate and streamline itself. So its overall trajectory will be slower and less efficient even if its profits are higher.

This big picture effect is why most economists agree that tariffs should be used very sparingly. They almost always cause unexpected damage, decrease overall employment and slow down an economy, but sometimes (like for food security or national defense) those costs are worth paying.

So Why is Donald Trump Throwing Around Tariffs Like They Are The Best Thing Ever?

This has been confusing to almost everyone. If you take him at his word, he appears to have a Bizarro Opposite Universe belief system about economics. Donald has claimed in speeches that the tariffs will somehow make us wealthier. He’s focusing on the first-order effects like GM hiring more workers, while completely ignoring the fact that everything else in the country gets less efficient in exchange.

But when he announces larger tariffs, share prices go down, because everyone who actually runs or invests in US companies knows that of course they will make less money on average. When tariffs are paused or reduced, share prices go back up. Yet he keeps wielding the threats and we go back and forth.

It seems to be obvious to everyone except Donald himself that Tariffs are just a national sales tax rather than some clever sneaky strategic weapon, which leads to various theories that okay, maybe he knows that too but is just pretending in order to gain some influence.

So right now our entire economy is subject to the whims of a single person.. And as long as this is the case, we’re just the same as any other dictatorship – something our constitution was supposed to prevent with the whole “three independent branches of government” thing.

But presidents have tried to break out of their constitutional cage and get more power many times in the past, and this is just the latest example. The real test will be if our system eventually manages to stop this abuse and put itself back in balance as it always has in the past. You can already see this fight beginning to play out in our court system, in this Economist article:

Even without the 145% nonsense numbers that were thrown around a few months ago, they are still far higher than they have been in the last 75 years or more. While it would be hard to pin down the current numbers in a stationary blog post like this one, the key thing to remember is that our current US economy is built around very low tariffs and relatively free trade.

Why haven’t I noticed Prices Going Up Yet?

While the US economy is fueled by a constant stream of cargo ships, as a whole we function like the biggest cargo ship of all: we have a huge inventory and it takes a while to change directions.

So in normal times, we already have several months of inventory of most things in the country. And then when all this drama started, importers started placing even more orders to stockpile things in advance before the tariffs hit. And now that they are in place, we’re importing a lot less stuff.

For now, we’re still using up the stockpiled inventory, but imports have dropped significantly so we’re quickly running out of cheap goods. If that happens, we will probably start seeing shortages and price increases throughout this summer or fall. For some things like plastic party trinkets, we can do just fine without. But if we lose access to core useful things like tools and machinery, the economic consequences will be much less fun.

The most important phrase to remember in US politics and economics is the phrase “This too shall pass.” The only mystery right now is that we don’t know exactly how it will pass. So we could sketch out a few scenarios:

1) The current crazy-high tariffs really do stick around:

I personally think this is the less likely scenario because nobody really wants it. But just as a thought experiment, it might go something like this:

2) They do end up being just a negotiating tactic and we go back to mostly low tariffs.

In other words, the best way to win the tariff game is not to play it.

Just as much of US prosperity is built upon our huge population of 330 million people living in 50 states with open borders and no trade restrictions, all (friendly) countries of the world can benefit from the free exchange of goods, services and even people. We’re all human beings and if we treat each other with a collaborative respect, we all grow richer.

I started writing this article on April 2nd, when Donald announced his “Liberation Day” and the stock market reacted with the biggest drop since 1932. Some people panicked and locked in big losses despite decades of warnings from your favorite financial bloggers, like this unfortunate soul in the comments to a JL Collins post:

But as I watched over the next two months, we have bounced our way back up – with each drop in proposed tariffs triggering a corresponding increase in stock prices (a measure of investor enthusiasm of how bright our future looks).

Right now, the US stock market is just about back to its all-time high. This doesn’t match with our current level of tariffs, which are still about seven times higher than they were before the circus opened. But it shows that investors believe it’s all going to end with a truce and a resumption of free-ish international trade.

If they’re wrong, the roller coaster ride will still have some more fun in store for us. But as long as we eventually end our current experiment in “emergency” tariff dictatorship and get back to functioning as a democracy, things should be just fine in the long run. I’m still 100% invested myself, so that’s where I place my bet.

The Biggest Lesson: Don’t Form Your Opinions Based on News Headlines

Decades ago in a brighter age of journalism, there may have been a time when headlines were designed primarily to inform us, with just a bit of sizzle and spice to pull in our attention. Unfortunately, nowadays the priorities have flipped where the primary goal is attention, and accuracy carries little or no weight. Even a totally inaccurate article makes money for the publisher.

So while Democrats and Republicans like to do battle over which media sources are biased, in reality they’re all wrong: all click-funded commercial media is biased – sometimes politically but even more importantly biased towards generating outrage and fear, because those generate more money.

1) Either ignore the media completely and focus on your own life, or

2) Become a subject matter expert on things you really care about, and then read the original sources whenever you want to learn about something.

I mostly practice option #1, but as a science and technology nerd I get into #2 in just the areas I find most interesting. And it’s amazing how the more deeply you understand a subject, the more you see just how wrong most media stories are about your area of expertise. Which means they’re probably pretty wrong about almost everything.

So as always, with this lesson learned it’s time to shut down that phone and laptop, exhale all our worries and get back outside with your real-life family and friends. See you in a few months!

Great question – I tried to cover this in the article under the heading, “Why haven’t I noticed prices going up yet?”

First of all, most of the tariffs (or threatened tariffs) haven’t even hit yet.

But even when they do, the end result will be a bit unpredictable. Importers can of course shift supply to countries with lower tariffs or even domestic suppliers. Consumers will also react to rising prices by scaling back their spending, which shifts prices back down the supply/demand curve a little.

In the extreme case, high tariffs can even cause a recession which lowers demand for almost all goods and services, which means that prices for domestically produced services with elastic pricing might go down and bring the overall inflation numbers back in check. In other words, some people lose their jobs so on average there’s less money being spent on restaurants -> restaurants have to lower their prices.

Heck, in a good enough recession even house prices and rents will drop, which is the biggest factor in the inflation basket.

Might be semantic, but maybe tariffs are not “inflation”. It would be like saying that a VAT would be inflationary. Instead, this is a one-time step-function change in the cost of goods, then inflation (velocity) resumes on the new cost base. Oren Cass had an interesting blog article on this last week. At least food for thought – he posits that economists don’t actually think tariffs are inflationary.

100% the case. Inflation is caused by an increase in the money supply, by definition. It means your purchasing power is worth less. A one-time increase in a specific category of goods of 15% is not “inflation.” Meanwhile, every time the government uses printed (or digitally entered) dollars to spend trillions they don’t have, inflation grows massively and compounds, and for some reason, the majority of people don’t bat an eye.

A great analogy for inflation would be something like this… You are in charge of the county fair. There are a bunch of vendors of popcorn, cotton candy, and ride like ferris wheels, etc. You print tickets that visitors can use to acquire these goods and ride these rides, and the vendors set their own ticket prices. You and your friends discover you can give yourselves tickets and get more popcorn and ride more rides since you own the ticket machine. With the flood of tickets, the vendors realize they can (and need to) raise their prices. This is inflation. And it doesn’t matter if it’s due to your and your friends doing it for yourselves, or just doing it because of more guests coming to the fair (for “growth”).

I think the definition of inflation is a rise in prices not a rise in money supply. Money supply is one factor in that, but so is the overall supply and demand of everything that is for sale. Money supply is increased or decreased as needed in reaction to what’s happening with prices, in order to keep prices more stable, if the system is well managed.

In your county fair example, you are holding the number of vendors and the items and quantities for sale as a constant while increasing the number of tickets. In reality the fair’s mini-economy will grow and shrink over time, and if the ticket supply were forced to always stay constant the ticket prices of rides, popcorn and cotton candy would move up and down significantly in reaction.

“I think the definition of inflation is a rise in prices not a rise in money supply.”

No it’s not wrong. Inflation is prices going higher as time passes. The causes of inflation are debatable, but “inflation” is a word that refers to prices going up regardless of the cause.

It’s possible for money supply to increase without inflation. Japanese deflation and lost decades are a prime example.

One interesting note, on top of your spot on analysis of the impact of tariffs, is how hard economic data, as traditionally collected, is to interpret in 2025.

Specifically, the unemployment rate is really interesting to me.

Clearly, the prevailing sentiment is that it’s a tough market out there for most (but not all) employees. At BiggerPockets, we were getting TONS of applicants for every available job posting for months.

But, yet, the employment reports show low unemployment, and jobs added with each passing month. What gives?

I believe that the answer lies in the gig economy and with self-employed workers. There are some 50 million Americans working gig work, self-employed, or who work as contractors. Contrary to popular belief, there are many of this cohort who actively choose that lifestyle and prefer it over a full-time job, getting a better mixture of total income and flexibility.

However, when that work becomes harder and harder, and it is no longer feasible to support yourself or your family on your combined uber, amazon delivery, lyft, and doordash routine, you begin to take that unappealing job for $45K per year.

You are now worse off, in terms of total income and flexibility.

But the employment report shows it as a net positive.

I believe that this effect does two things:

1) Presents a false view of the economy as healthier than it actually is. 2) Gives the federal reserve free reign to be extra cautious about lowering rates – inflation is a bigger threat than the “jobs” report that they are mandated to watch.

Thank you for raising this point. The lack of concern about the impacts on businesses has been a real source of frustration for me.

My day job has given me a window into some industry sectors, including during Trump 1.0 and the trade war then. I always remember the small US steel manufacturer one of my colleagues spoke with at that time, when researching some of the impacts of steel tariffs.

The company was an important employer in its local area, producing steel canisters that it sold to a global slate of companies (so it was an exporter, and also sold domestically). Its main input was a particular type of steel pipe made in China (so it was also an importer). After Trump implemented steel tariffs, this small firm was suddenly paying an additional $250 million (back in 2018/2019; do your own inflation math as to what that would be today) at the US border before it could pick up a shipment.

It wasn’t going to be able to afford to stay open if it couldn’t get the administration to give it a tariff exemption (something Trump 1.0 was more willing to do, although the time involved to apply and, hopefully, get some sort of relief (many didn’t) meant companies were shelling out cash in the meantime). Why? Because not only did it not have a way to source the pipe in the US (steel is made to specification and you often can’t just readily swap things out), it couldn’t afford to do that because with a global client base, it needed to keep its pricing competitive (its customers could seek out non-US sources, unaffected by tariffs, for canisters instead).

We do actually have a manufacturing sector in the US. Most companies in that sector are small and midsized firms (fewer than 500 workers; often much smaller) and these may be important employers locally (although most employment in the industry overall is via the smaller number of very large firms); many are family firms. All sizes of manufacturer may import a raw material, a component or a finished good (including capital equipment for their facilities). When we tariff, we end up hurting our own manufacturing sector along the way. I lost track of the steel canister-maker’s fate, but I’ve never forgotten its difficulty, as just one illustration of tariff impacts that aren’t about the CPI.

But there’s also no real controversy (among people who study this stuff) in saying that tariffs tend to raise prices somewhere along the way, although it can take several months and may not be a straight $1 for $1 increase for end-consumers (although it often, eventually, is). I agree that it doesn’t create a prolonged rise in inflation (which is a rate of increase), but it does tend to eventually raise prices over a certain period and they then stay at that higher level. That’s actually part of how tariffs work, by putting a new floor under prices, reducing price competition.

And there are spillovers well beyond the firms initially impacted. For instance, US makers of tin plate, used in can-making, were hit by Trump 1.0’s steel tariffs, which jacked up their input costs (whether they continued with imports or switched to domestic sources — especially since domestic steel makers raised their own prices after tariffs were imposed on imports, an approach they’ve continued with in the latest trade war). This then made foreign-produced end-products such as canned food more attractive, because the pricing was better due to the lower production costs for non-US producers of tin plate. In other words, not only did US tin plate manufacturers suffer, but so did their US customers, as those companies’ customers looked elsewhere. (Trump’s much-broader trade war this time could offset some of this, by making imported canned goods more expensive, as well, depending on how things play out, which, in turn, would affect things like grocery store margins, etc.)

I also want to add that one of the biggest problems worrying the manufacturing industry for years, including pre-pandemic, has been the difficulty firms often face in filling the jobs they already have, and the difficulty they expect to face in filling jobs they expect to have due to a looming wave of retirements. This is due to several reasons: a skills gap (applicants not having the desired skill-sets); geographic miss-matches (jobs in one place, potential workers in another); problems with drug use in some communities (applicants are often expected to pass drug tests in order to operate machinery; the opioid epidemic has truly clobbered some communities in manufacturing areas); lack of interest among younger people in going into manufacturing or other production sectors (definitely something we need to work on; lack of exposure and training in K-12 is part of the trouble there, although the appeal of other types of work has also pulled potential workers elsewhere — maybe AI taking white collar jobs will sort that out?); and an increasing tightness in the overall US labor market due to demographics (ie, retirements on the aggregate, although jobs involving manual labor often see retirements at earlier ages, skewing the problem for those industries).

To finally conclude this overlong comment — which still barely scratches the surface; I didn’t even go into the tariff (and trade war) impacts on US shipping and logistics sectors tied to global trade, including imports — a major and rarely-discussed downside of tariffs is simply that it’s so difficult to readily see the ways they thread through an economy and create a drag on firms’ employment, wages/benefits, expansion plans, financing options, earnings and stock prices, and, yes, on consumer spending. The hits to businesses are often below the radar — especially since many companies don’t want to attract the anger of protectionists (unions; certain parts of the progressive wing; the Trump administration) by openly admitting how tariffs hurt their business. So people who aren’t trade geeks are understandably oblivious to real effects of these types of policies. As Cullen Roche over at Discipline Funds has repeatedly put it, with tariffs, you have less economic growth than you would have had — you just don’t know it.

The Biden administration and Dems in Congress (and sometimes even GOPers in Congress at that time, in some rare moments of bipartisanship) did several good things to directly support certain manufacturing and other production sectors (in my world I knew about policy for clean energy-related manufacturing; the defense industry; critical minerals; computer chips). Trump and the GOP have reduced or eliminated a chunk of that, unfortunately. But the recent tax bill did include some useful items for manufacturing. The GOP could do even more to directly support the sector, if manufacturing jobs are the real goal of all this, without the downsides of tariffs. (To be clear, this is not a political argument that I’m making; I didn’t like the tariffs imposed during the Biden admin, any more than Trump’s.)

Current US Debt ($36.2 trillion Source: https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/datasets/historical-debt-outstanding/historical-debt-outstanding

2016 Nominal US GDP Growth (3.2%) Source: https://www.jec.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/34c0c783-f785-459c-a93a-2997c6abb8b4/01-30-gdp-review.pdf

2019 Nominal US GDP Growth (4.1%) Source: https://www.bea.gov/news/2020/gross-domestic-product-fourth-quarter-and-year-2019-advance-estimate#:~:text=Current%2Ddollar%20GDP%20increased%204.1,table%201%20and%20table%203).

US Federal deficit as percentage of GDP Source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FYFSGDA188S

Also, I think it’s worth flagging the US debt as a proportion of GDP, which is the key statistic vs. just thinking of the absolute figure. There are different ways to slice the US debt, but they all tell the same story. Just taking the basic total US debt relative to GDP shows a rise from 54% at year ending 2000 to 121% as of 1Q2025. That is staggeringly scary. Source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GFDEGDQ188S

Another after thought, while nominal GDP matters for the annual deficit, that is not to say real GDP doesn’t matter in a silo. They both have relevance. Clearly the US government has more control over expenses, and to a somewhat lesser extent revenue, than it does inflation. For 2024, the deficit ran at 6.28% of GDP. If inflation, which most of us can agree above a low percentage is typically bad, drops back into a ~2% range but real GDP growth runs in the 2-3% range, which is decent growth, then we’re still only growing nominal GDP at 4-5% vs. 6%+ under the state-of-play. This is an interesting analysis. The way I summed it up to an acquaintance is that Trump is playing with fire. In the end, it may be that we have something nice and shiny as a result. However, it is just as likely (if not more) that this whole thing is a dumpster fire and in the end it will just a smoking heap of ash.

However, the more fundamental problem here is that the reason that things like this (i.e., Trump unilaterally going tariff-nuclear, which is actually quite similar to what Biden did trying to illegally wipe out student loan debt, it’s just that Trump’s actions are at a different order of magnitude) is because Congress actively refuses to do their jobs. In the last several decades they have rather been rather determined to pass really loose/broad laws and specifically leave the “details” to the executive branch (either as some nebulous presidential power, or via some rule-making provision for an executive agency). This was bad but not terrible as long as we were electing presidents who were within a standard deviation of the ‘center’ of the political spectrum. However, Trump is a major outlier, and now it is readily apparent that Congress’ approach of letting the executive branch decide most things for itself isn’t actually a really good idea.

Even going back to the difference between Trump’s use of tariffs and Biden’s student debt cancellation efforts, it is clear that Biden’s policy, while objectively of very dubious legality, didn’t move the macroeconomic needle. Trump’s policies, on the other hand, even if they turn out to be completely legal (which I’m not sure they will), are rather painful object lesson on why Congress needs to actually do their jobs with a bit more effort.

A stray bit of additional perspective: A good friend of mine lost a large swath of her extended family when covid churned through northern Italy in the first year of the pandemic. Communities in their area suffered terrible losses that upended the social fabric overall, in addition to the grief suffered by specific families.

This also happened in many parts of the US, with certain kinds of communities hit particularly hard (groups that tend to live with extended family were especially vulnerable; non-hispanic white middle- and upper-class America is least-likely to live that way, so people from that type of background may not have seen much of this directly).

Given what NYC itself went through early in that first year, it also wouldn’t surprise me if NYT staffers genuinely felt horrified at what was happening. My friends and colleagues living in NYC certainly felt that way, based on what they were seeing and experiencing directly themselves.

So yes, it’s absolutely true that all forms of heart disease combined remained the number one cause of death in both 2020 and 2021, followed by all cancers combined. But I suspect that many people whose families and communities were gutted by covid would agree with the NYT that the toll from that new cause of death was terrible, and that it was something worth being concerned about, even if covid alone ended up being the third-leading cause of US deaths in both of those years, after which broad herd immunity finally set in.

Also, if anyone has an idea for how to fund newspaper journalism such that eyeballs aren’t the thing, I know several very good journalists who would *love* to hear what it is. (Pricier subscriptions can’t be the answer; not if you want to pay decent salaries and thus keep people around so that you have a good mix of entry-level people and experienced folks, and not if you want to include small and regional news outlets in your funding model — you could never charge enough for subscriptions for a local or even regional paper for that to cover all costs and still have a decent staff, both in terms of actual size and experience mix. This applies to both digital and hard-copy papers.)

If you do not think that the NYT serves a political agenda, the you are naïve.

And while I think that Pete’s nostalgic comment (“Decades ago in a brighter age of journalism, there may have been a time when headlines were designed primarily to inform us…”) is equally naïve, he recognizes that today news organizations are driven by getting eyeballs on their content. The thing is, it’s always been like this. Certainly, the intensity has varied with times and places, but yellow journalism (the type of sensationalism that characterizes nearly 100% of mass media coverage today) originated in the 1880s in NYC. Back then the NYT didn’t lower themselves to that level, but it’s pretty obvious that today they are down there and they deserve to be compared to the likes of FoxNews, MSNBC, and so forth.

I think a useful comparison that illustrates something important about the NYT is to look at its news articles and compare them with those in the Wall Street Journal (owned by News Corp, by the way, as is Fox News). Both the NYT and WSJ are dealing with a crazy-ass environment for “newspapers” vs back in the day. And both approach their news journalism in a similar way, even if the specific type of news story they do may differ.

At the same time, nothing could be more different than their respective opinion sections — both the editorials by their editorial boards and those by columnists and guests are 180-degrees opposite from each other much of the time.

In other words, in terms of political-ish stance, they are radically different. In terms of journalism? Pretty similar: fact-based, attempting to give a full picture, and corrections if someone messes something up. They entertain if they can, but it’s secondary to information provision.

I can’t say the same about Fox News (which I used to watch some years ago, but stopped when I realized I was never really going to get a full picture of anything since it wasn’t their style). They are really an entertainment-first entity, and they are facing fierce competition from Newsmax, which has made it less and less appealing for them to say anything they think their viewers might not want to hear. (That said, I’ve found the online version of their sister product, Fox Business, to be helpful at times. Just as I like CNBC’s “state of freight” pages for some aspects of tariff impacts on shipping and warehousing. Written! Not the videos/cable shows for either of these. There’s usually more information in written material, and the potential for more nuance. (Not always fulfilled, alas).)

With all due respect, you, and unfortunately, many others, are missing the point.

We (and Trump) get that the cost will get passed onto the consumers. Or at least that’s the “first order effect” (to borrow your phrase.)

What you’re missing is that consumers get to decide between whether to purchase the item or not. If they are willing to eat the cost, and the item is something they absolutely can’t live without, they’ll buy it. Or they won’t buy it at all.

In the latter case, the sales numbers (and thus revenue) of the company selling the goods will drop. At which point that company has a choice to make: live with the drop in sales, and thus bottom line, eat part of the tariff or all of it, in order to increase volume.

Obviously, the company’s goal (let’s use Nike as an example), is to make as much money as possible. So if they naively pass 100% of the cost onto the consumer, their sales might drop so much that they’ll realize that wasn’t the best financial decision. This is an optimization problem: find the global maximum. The variables are: what % of tariffs to eat (vs pass on), whether to continue to offshore or onshore (and to what degree), and so on.

Using the Nike example (because they recently sobbed about their $1Bn tariff bill), their product is, among other things, athletic shoes. They’re not an essential item. They’re a luxury. It’s also not something you buy every week. Consumers can easily forego purchasing a new pair of Nike shoes, and Nike can decide if it can stomach the sales drop or not and react accordingly. That’s not our concern. We shouldn’t feel sorry for Nike who got rich at the expense of exploiting sweat job labor and pocketing the enormous margins, while selling out American jobs.

The other second-order effect you missed is the fact that by creating these “tariff walls” the money stays onshore. I.e. customers buy US-made goods and pay local companies, i.e. their fellow citizen. The money feeds back into the US economy. Without them, even though goods are “cheaper” for the consumer, the money flows out of the country: enriching China and other third world countries at our expense. What are some third-order effects you think might arise from that? I hope you see how this thinking is a bit short-sighted.

Of course, if one’s goals are not to support and protect the USA and its people, then the above will seem silly and pointless (or even absurd!). But of course I’m writing this with the (naive) assumption that a US citizen cares about the well-being of their country and fellow citizen (I know, crazy.)

Your analysis was overly simplistic which had you naively conclude that Trump is a raving idiot when perhaps you’re missing a substantial portion of what is really going on.

Also, I did not quite understand the point of money flowing out being a process that enriches other countries. A trade deficit means that the other countries are receiving more money than they are paying. But what do they then do with it? First, “they” here means the central banks of the other countries as the companies that receive the dollars for the stuff they sell to the US will trade it to the central bank for their local currency. So the central banks of the other countries are amassing an immense amount of dollars which they are not spending on buying US products due to the trade deficit. And judging from data from these central banks, they seem to be doing mainly one thing with these. Buying US treasury bonds. Which I find interesting, because these bonds will return more dollars which they then spend on buying more bonds because the US is not producing enough interesting-to-them goods or services to trade these dollars for.

Sounds like actually a good system from US perspective to me? Buy stuff from the other countries for dollars and they will give these dollars back in the form of US treasury bonds that can be used by the US government to then again spend within the US, for building infrastructure or paying social security.

And we all know how the US treasury bonds will be paid back when they come due. By selling more US treasury bonds. Which seem to be in good demand as the central banks of all the other countries want to put their dollars to use in some way.

I think I once heard a saying: If you owe 2 million dollars to the bank, the bank owns you. If you owe 2 trillion dollars, you own the bank.

Replace “you” by “US” and “bank” by “other countries” in that and the whole situation looks actually quite good from an US perspective to me. So looking back, should one really be surprised of what Nixon did in 1971 ( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nixon_shock )? I mean, why would the others buy treasury bonds that only give them back more dollars when they could trade the dollars they buy the bonds with for gold?

Can you please elaborate on in what way you see other countries being enriched by this system?

It’s important to highlight that whilst all tariffs are sales taxes, not all sales taxes are tariffs. VAT for example, is most definitely not a tariff (or even non-tariff trade barrier) as it’s applied equally to imported and domestically produced goods and services. The average tariffs the European Union charged on U.S. exports were less than 2 percent, so there’s nothing reciprocal about Trump’s tariffs.

Tariffs were the original taxation vehicle for the Federal government, because they are a tax on consumption (vs production) and because they are quickly self-limiting; consumption of imported goods is far more elastic than earning an income and so government revenue from them falls quickly as tariffs rise “too high”. States are limited by competition. The 16th amendment uncapped the size of federal government and now here we stand. This Is The Summer To Tick Santorini Off The Bucket List

📅 2025-06-03  |  Read Source →

It’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

In the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

But now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

And the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

The trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up quickly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

As an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

Naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.

Virgin Atlantic Ups The Ante In India, As The World Dials In

📅 2025-06-03  |  Read Source →

This week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India. In Virgin fashion, it’s doing so in style, with a joint announcement among partners Delta Airlines, Air France-KLM, and a new strategic partner IndiGo.

On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the new strategic partnership for India was announced with very interesting nods to the future.

IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.

That’s probably a good thing, because with recent service additions, Virgin now flies a million seats a year to India and it sounds like others are piling on more flights too. It’s now one of the largest operators to India.

I’ve been bullish on India as the next great center of the world for a while now. It’s not necessarily that I’m at all intelligent, it’s just based on the fact that India is the world’s largest population. But, when Ed Bastian, Delta’s formidable CEO says it, people tend to listen. Bastian mentioned India being the most important aviation market globally now and signaled a return of direct services for the carrier as well.

Virgin has been a small step ahead, adding service regularly on their Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore routes. IndiGo chose this alliance over formidable competition and this will certainly be a space to watch as more global airlines and alliances focus on India.

Geo-political activity points to India becoming a new manufacturing super power, in addition to its prolific work in tech, IT and customer service, not to mention blossoming tourism. These kind of globally connected businesses are big business, huge in fact, for corporate contracts and easy onward connectivity to regional sites is essential. The partnership makes sense.

In a somewhat rare and impressive signal of unity and seriousness towards India, Virgin Atlantic made their India crews part of the core Virgin family, rather than as contractors through a third party local company, known in aviation world as a GSA. This means Virgin’s India crews are a part of the full team, with benefits too.

When asked about loyalty implications of the new alliance, Virgin Atlantic CEO, Shai Weiss, noted a mutual passion for using loyalty to enhance guest experience far beyond just the earn and burn of points and miles. For future iterations, they’ve offered the following…

The MoU (memorandum of understanding) also creates a framework for deeper collaboration between the carriers on a bilateral and multilateral basis; contemplates commercial collaboration including network, loyalty, cargo and sales, subject to regulatory approvals; explores areas of non-commercial cooperation including aircraft maintenance, sustainability, training, ground handling; and acknowledges the need to develop advanced collaboration through use of technology to efficiently service joint customers.

IndiGo will provide onward connectivity for Virgin and the other strategic partners to 32 destinations, making it easier than ever to see Udaipur, Jaipur, Mumbai, Kashmir and delights further south in Bangalore and Goa.

I just returned from the lovely Leela Palace in Delhi, as I watched the news happen live.

To me, India is a country of joy. Even people with truly nothing seem to find positivity and it’s generally a way of life here. Hospitality is as warm and steeped in tradition as it comes, too. It’s hot, it’s humid, but it’s an experience unlike any other and that’s something that’s harder to say these days than I’d like.

The food, ugh. I adore. Sure, I’ll take a dosa from the South over a heavy curry from the North most days, but I love both and if you don’t love a good black daahl there’s something wrong with you.

In short, it’s already fairly easy to get to India but it’s about to get a whole lot easier and not just to hub cities too. More seats means more chances to use points, by the way!

Best Car Vacuums of 2026

📅 2025-04-17  |  Read Source →

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

We put the top car vacuums to the test on a dusty-but-beloved Porsche Boxster. Here’s what sucked (in a good way).

This article was updated in November 2026.

A clean car is a happy car, but you need the right vacuum to keep things tidy. (As an outdoor adventurer and proud pet owner, I know this all too well.) So, do I really need a special vacuum just for my car? Yes. That’s why I was excited to put a fleet of top-rated car vacuums to the test on a dusty Porsche Boxster at our garage in New Jersey. After deciding which units we wanted to focus on, we assessed suction power, ease of use, hose length, portability, attachment versatility, and overall quality. A good vacuum should make detailing effortless, not frustrating.

Whether you just want to tidy up or are a serious detailer, these are the car vacuums that stood out in our hands-on testing. Each proved they can handle everything from fine road dirt to the stubborn fur of a rambunctious dog. If it made our list, it’s because we’d use it ourselves.

More Car-Care Gear: Best Leather Car Cleaners | Best Upholstery Cleaners | Best Interior Cleaners

The Metrovac Vac N Blo isn’t just a car vacuum. This machine is a steel-bodied detailer with a 4-hp motor that delivers serious suction and blower power. The two flexible six-foot hoses aren’t flimsy plastic cords; they’re made with a pro-grade material for those who take cleaning seriously.

Right out of the box, it impressed with its array of attachments: two extension wands, four deluxe micro-detailing attachments, a blower nozzle, a pick-all upholstery nozzle, a dust brush, and a crevice tool.

Whether you’re dealing with deep-seated pet hair, stubborn crumbs, or layers of dust, this vacuum does its job with ease. There was a noticeable difference even after just one go-over on the floor mat. The Vac N Blo never felt like it struggled, wherever we were vacuuming.

When you need to dry your car or blast grit out of vents, the blower function is just as powerful, making it a true two-in-one garage essential. I used this setting to blow the bits of dirt and gravel right out of the garage door.

It also allows you the option to attach wheels, making it even easier to maneuver. In this case, I attached the shoulder strap and had it move with me as I worked my way around the mats and car. It’s also a very sleek design—it looked sharp in the garage and stood out not just in performance but also in aesthetics.

Beyond its power, the all-metal construction gives it a level of durability you won’t find in typical car vacuums. The long hose and multiple attachments make tackling every inch of your interior easy, turning a once-dreaded task into a precision operation. If you want a vacuum that’ll deliver professional-level results, the Metrovac Vac N Blo is the one to get.

The DetailVac is the smallest on the list, and it was also the easiest to work with. It plugged right into the Boxster’s 12-volt outlet and, at only three pounds, was easy to maneuver. The 16-foot cord is long enough to accommodate a bigger vehicle with multiple seats or crevices. Overall, it does what it states but doesn’t excel.

While it picked up most of the dust and dirt on the floor mats, it left behind pet fur and debris. The vacuum includes three attachments that are helpful in harder-to-reach spots: The crevice tool worked well, but the brush tool didn’t do much for puppy fur. A flexible connection hose also acts as an extended hose, but it seemed to diminish the suction power when added. It’s not as powerful as the others we tested, which makes sense given its size.

I liked that an additional air filter was included. Depending on how often you use the vacuum, the filters can last up to six months without needing a change, but it’s nice that an extra one is provided.

Overall, the DetailVac is convenient and great for quick cleanups or accidents. I think it would be especially helpful if you have kids.

The Bissell Garage Pro Wall-Mounted Wet/Dry Vacuum is for anyone serious about keeping their car and garage clean. Mounted on your wall with a 32-foot hose, it delivers strong 12-amp suction to tackle dirt and wet spills. There’s a blower option, perfect for drying off a freshly washed Porsche, which I did with stellar results.

Even at its size, assembly was simple. Once it’s together, it performs at the level you’d expect from a professional detailing station. This is the best pick if you have the room and use a vacuum in your garage often. It’s a full-service garage vacuum built to take a beating and deliver strong suction for any surface of your vehicle.

What also sets it apart is its auto-tool kit, which includes attachments—crevice tools, upholstery brushes, and a wet nozzle for moisture cleanup—for every cleaning scenario.

Whether you’re an obsessive detailer or just want a cleaner ride, the Garage Pro delivers. It is powerful, versatile, and a worthwhile addition to any garage.

Adam’s Polishes Wall-Mounted Vacuum packs a lot of power for a smaller unit. I quickly understood why most people use the wall-mount option; not only does it help keep the 30-foot hose out of the way, but it also helps keep your garage organized. If I had mounted this, the hose probably would’ve been less cumbersome to maneuver. Drilling holes in our space to mount several vacuums was not an option, but we did our best to re-create this real-world scenario. Assembly was a bit of a struggle—especially getting the central hose in—but I might not have used enough force initially. My advice would be to use all your strength; I promise you won’t break it.

The suction is decent, with 120 volts of power, but the attachments really help this vacuum shine: steel telescoping wand, bare-floor tool, snake wand, crevice tool, elongated dust brush, and upholstery tool. They make this vacuum even more versatile, allowing you to tackle everything from floor mats to delicate surfaces efficiently.

Using this vacuum was genuinely satisfying, like power-washing your interior with suction. Adam’s did indeed get the job done fast, and had it been wall-mounted, I think I would’ve seen its overall appeal, since using the hose would likely be more manageable. Adam’s Polishes Wall-Mounted Vacuum is worth every penny for those who love organization.

The Shark StainForce isn’t your typical car vacuum, and that’s precisely why we wanted to include it. Rather than tackling loose dirt, this cordless spot cleaner focuses on stubborn oil stains, soda spills, and odors embedded in your car’s carpeting.

There’s a three-step cleaning process involved, but it’s well worth the extra work. Spray the affected area with Shark’s dual-activated cleaning solution, scrub with the included attachment, and use the vacuum’s suction to extract the mess. The dual-chamber formula mixes when sprayed, helping break down stains without requiring any measuring or extra preparation. Two attachments, including a crevice tool, make it easier to reach tight spaces around seats and other interior surfaces.

Weighing under three pounds, the StainForce is easy to maneuver, and its cordless design eliminates the hassle of finding an outlet. The included storage caddy keeps everything organized between cleanups.

There are a few limitations. Battery life topped out at approximately 20 minutes when we tested (so it still works fine for spot cleaning). Also, you’ll need to purchase Shark’s own cleaning solution when the included supply runs out.

For drivers regularly battling coffee spills, muddy footprints, or pet accidents, the StainForce offers a convenient, targeted cleaning solution.

A high-quality vacuum cleaner can make all the difference for keeping your car’s interior spotless. Unlike household vacuums, car-specific models are designed to tackle heavier debris in tight spaces. However, with so many options available, choosing the right one can be overwhelming. It’s important to consider key features that affect performance and convenience to make an informed decision.

Three of the most crucial factors to evaluate are suction power, which determines how effectively the vacuum picks up dirt; attachments and accessories, which help clean hard-to-reach areas; and the power source, which impacts portability and run time.

Understanding these features will help you find a vacuum that best suits your needs, whether you prioritize strong suction for deep cleaning, versatile tools for detail work, or the malleability of a hose. Let’s dive into these essential features to ensure you choose the right car vacuum cleaner for the job.

Suction power is the most critical factor in a car vacuum because vehicle interiors can become a nightmare with everything we drag in and out of them. Unlike home carpets, car surfaces are filled with a million little spaces, textured upholstery, and stubborn floor mats that anything you can think of clings to. A vacuum with weak suction won’t be able to extract dirt that’s ground into these surfaces, leaving your car looking only half clean. Not ideal.

Additionally, higher suction power means faster, more efficient cleaning. Instead of repeatedly going over the same spot, a strong vacuum gets the job done in fewer passes, saving you time and effort. It also helps tackle heavier things such as leaves, sand, or pebbles. If you take your car’s cleanliness seriously (or don’t want to spend forever vacuuming), a high-powered vacuum is the way to go.

Attachments and accessories are essential in a car vacuum because car interiors are full of tight spaces and tricky surfaces that a standard nozzle can’t handle. Unlike home vacuums, which deal with flat carpets and open areas, a car vacuum must navigate between seats, air vents, and cup holders, all of which require specialized tools.

For example, a crevice tool helps reach between and along door panels, while a brush attachment is perfect for loosening dust from dashboards. Wide nozzles quickly work on large areas like a trunk, and wet/dry tools handle accidents before they become permanent stains. The right attachments don’t just make cleaning easier; they ensure you’re getting every last crumb out of your ride, leaving it truly spotless.

The power source of a car vacuum determines its suction strength, mobility, and convenience. Corded (AC-powered) vacuums offer the strongest suction but require an outlet and may limit movement. Cordless (battery-powered) models provide maximum portability for quick cleanups but often have weaker suction and limited run time.

Vacuums that plug into a car’s 12-volt outlet are great for on-the-go use but generally lack the power of AC models. Choosing the right type depends on your needs, such as going corded for power, cordless for convenience, or 12-volt for in-car accessibility.

The ThisWorx portable car vacuum routinely came up as the one to avoid. Its low suction didn’t do much, leaving most of the dirt and dust behind. While it is inexpensive, you do indeed get what you pay for.

The same goes for generic no-name vacuums on Amazon. While they are more affordable, they are also unreliable and often break within months of purchase.

We focused on suction power, attachments, and ease of use for this test. Using substantially dirty floor mats as our starting point, we taped them off to determine which vacuum was the most powerful. These mats were full of dirt, dust, pebbles, and dog fur; they were pretty much littered with what you might encounter in your vehicle. This strategy helped us quickly determine which vacuums were up to the task.

Our garage in New Brunswick, New Jersey, was the ideal backdrop for this test. Not only was it still dirty from summer trips, it also allowed me to spread out the old and very used floor mats I’d be using. While this test focused on how effectively the vacuums would clean up cars, a happy surprise was that they also cleaned the garage.

For this test, we reached out to pros to see what products they prefer. After determining fan favorites, digging around forums, and connecting with detailers we’ve worked with in the past, we devised a list of items to review. (You know you’re headed in the right direction when you hear the same brand or product come up multiple times.) This is how we arrived at Chemical Guys, Adam’s, Bissell, and Shark—solid and reliable brands. Metrovac popped up in my digging as a reliable shop vac in a popular Reddit group (r/AutoDetailing). They weren’t wrong.

We didn’t look at handheld car vacuums in this test. While they’re tops for convenience, they would be a separate category to investigate, given their variety. We did keep convenience in mind when picking the units we wanted to focus on, but this test was done with serious garage owners and car enthusiasts in mind.

When we reviewed the Car+Boat from Dyson, we were immensely impressed at how well the mini-vac lived up to its brand’s legacy. With legendary suction power, the Dyson was as much a revelation for car lovers as the company’s larger vacuums were for homeowners all those years ago.

Portable, lightweight, and affordable. What more could you want in a car vac? With a 20-volt MAX Li-ion battery and extra-long crevice tool, it’s as great for the car as it is around the house.

Looking for a little more power than a portable cordless vacuum can provide? Pick up this mini-utility shop vac from Armor All. It’s far more convenient than lugging around a larger shop vac, has a washable filter, and doubles as a blower.

When choosing a car or garage vacuum, size and capacity are crucial factors that impact performance and convenience. A vacuum with anywhere from two to six gallons of capacity is usually sufficient for car detailing, providing enough volume for typical debris while remaining lightweight and portable. Smaller vacuums are easier to maneuver inside a car and can be stored conveniently in a garage or trunk.

A 10-plus-gallon shop vacuum is better for garage use or frequent heavy-duty cleaning. These larger models can handle bigger messes, including sawdust, metal shavings, and wet spots, without requiring frequent emptying. They also typically feature more powerful motors for increased suction. However, they take up more storage space and may be less portable. If you need a balance between power and maneuverability, a mid-size vacuum can provide strong suction without being too bulky.

While a regular household vacuum might seem convenient for cleaning your car or garage, it often lacks the necessary power, durability, and specialized attachments for effective cleaning in these environments. Household vacuums are designed primarily for indoor surfaces such as carpets and hardwood floors, meaning they may struggle to pick up messes commonly found in cars and garages. Their shorter hoses and bulkier designs can make it challenging to reach tight spaces.

Dedicated car vacuums and shop vacuums are better suited for these tasks, offering more powerful suction, longer hoses, and attachments specifically designed for automotive cleaning. These vacuums are built with durability, often featuring rugged designs that can withstand dust, moisture, and rough handling in a garage setting. While household vacuums may work in a pinch for light cleaning, investing in a purpose-built car or garage vacuum ensures more efficient cleaning and a longer-lasting machine.

HEPA (high-efficiency particulate air) filters are essential when purchasing a car or garage vacuum, especially if you are concerned about air quality. Standard vacuum filters may struggle to trap fine particles such as dust, pollen, pet dander, and mold spores, which can get released back into the air during cleaning.

HEPA filters, however, are designed to capture at least 99.97 percent of particles, making them highly effective at reducing allergens and airborne contaminants. This is particularly beneficial if you suffer from allergies.

For car and garage cleaning, a HEPA or high-efficiency filtration system can also help keep your vehicle’s interior and your garage workspace cleaner by preventing fine dust from resettling. While HEPA-filtered vacuums may be slightly more expensive, they offer significant benefits for maintaining a healthier environment.
